problem: The low-speed behaviour of the gust line is stated backwards. The gust line starts at n = 1 at V = 0 and rises linearly with V, while the stall line rises as V² from n = 0. So at V_S1 and just above it the gust line lies above the stall line, not inside it. A gust load factor in that band cannot be reached at all, because the wing stalls first; the stall line governs there. The figure in this same chapter shows exactly this (at V = 60 m/s the gust line is at n = 2.01 while the stall limit is n ≈ 1.10), so text and figure contradict each other.
fix: Rewrite as: 'At low speed the gust line lies above the stall line, so those gust load factors cannot be reached — the wing stalls first and the stall line governs. The gust line crosses below the stall line at a higher speed V_B, which is at or above V_A. From there on the gust line is the boundary, and at high speed the increment grows with V so the gust line can rise above n_max.'

problem: The plotted gust line (60, 2.01) to (89, 2.5) lies above the stall line over its whole drawn length, and it meets n = 2.5 at V = 89 m/s while the stall line there allows only n = (89/57.14)² = 2.43. So the point where the gust line touches the flat top is outside the manoeuvre envelope: the aircraft cannot be at n = 2.5 at 89 m/s, because V_A is 90.4 m/s. A student reading the graph will place the gust corner below V_A, which is impossible.
fix: Choose a shallower gust line that crosses n = 2.5 at a speed at or above V_A, for example a line through (0, 1) with slope 0.0136 per m/s, giving n = 2.5 at about 110 m/s and crossing the stall line near 83 m/s. Draw only the part below the stall line and clip or dash the rest, so the corner where it meets the n = 2.5 top is a reachable point.

problem: The top boundary is drawn flat at n = 2.5 to 120 m/s and then slopes straight down to n = 0 at V_D = 160 m/s. That implies the permitted load factor falls to zero at the dive speed. In practice the top stays at n_max up to V_C and then reduces to a lower value (2.0 for transport aircraft) at V_D, after which the envelope closes steeply to the negative limit. Section 2 also never says that the top is not flat all the way to V_D.
fix: Change the upper limit to (90.4, 2.5) → (120, 2.5) → (160, 2.0), then close steeply to n_min at 160 m/s. Add one sentence in Section 2: 'From V_C to V_D the limit falls from n_max to a lower value, 2.0 for transport aircraft, and then the envelope closes steeply at V_D.'

problem: The formula given is the sharp-edged gust idealisation with no gust alleviation factor, but it is presented as the working design formula. Students will use it as the certification value, which it is not: the real increment is smaller because the aircraft is not a point mass and the lift build-up is unsteady.
fix: Add one sentence after the formula: 'This is the sharp-edged gust value. Certification work multiplies the increment by a gust alleviation factor K_g (below 1, from the aircraft mass ratio and wing loading), so the design gust line is shallower than this formula gives.'

problem: The answer stays vague ('can add a local load or a pitching load', 'can also trigger aeroelastic effects'). The standard reason is more definite: at V_D the aerodynamic forces are largest, and full deflection cases (control surface and tail loads) are separate design cases that can exceed the limit loads even when the aircraft load factor n stays below n_max.
fix: Answer: 'The V-n envelope limits the aircraft load factor, not the local loads from control deflection. At V_D the dynamic pressure is highest, so a sudden full deflection gives large hinge moments, tail loads and wing torsion. These full-deflection cases are checked separately and can be critical even when n is below n_max.'
